story_text.value:
Hey HN! Tried to show this off a couple times before but didn't really get much traction, figured now that more time's been spent in the UI/UX side of things I'd give it another shot.

This is my attempt, started at the beginning of the year, to build a complete Magic: The Gathering engine.

Instead of coding individual card scripts, a compiler takes oracle text as input and outputs the card definition itself into executable effects that ran in the engine.

Another cool thing which is mentioned in the title is that tournaments can be played without relying on a central server hosting the game, and without having to trust in your opponents playing honestly. Shuffles carry a ZKP so that all peers can verify they were performed securely, and even complex cards like Praetor's Grasp which give you information about your opponent's cards that they themselves don't have work as expected with perfect secrecy!

I'd love to get some feedback on HN, especially regarding broken mechanics/scenarios and whatever potential improvements you think are worth adding.

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I wanted to share this stylesheet for a skeuomorphic button that comes from a project I've been working on. Hope you find some interest in it

I wanted to capture some of the physicality of real buttons so I've been playing with this "soft divot" concept. It's a border style that creates an illusion of the button sitting flush on the page.

Skeuomorphic buttons have been around forever. What I think is different here is this idea of maintaining the button face on the same plane as its background.

It comes with three elevation levels: raised (+1), default (0) and sunken (-1). For primary actions you can choose the raised plane face. Then most other buttons, they can stay nicely on the default UI plane.

title.value: Show HN: Divot.css – a simple skeuomorphic button style

story_text.value:
Buy low in one city, travel, sell high. 15 days. Everyone plays the same market each day, and everyone ends up on the leaderboard.

I used to play Drug Lord 2 nearly 20 years ago and loved it! I forgot about it until recently when I accidentally stumbled across it again.

I'm a software engineer but also wanted to learn how to use Claude Code, so I challenged myself to make a similar game that was more family friendly. It's a web game designed to be played on a PC or phone.

It's vanilla TypeScript with no framework. The game engine is a set of pure functions driven by a seeded random-number generator, so the Cloudflare Worker can replay every submitted run move by move to verify the score before it reaches the leaderboard. The whole thing runs on Cloudflare's free tier.

I've put a lot of effort into the leaderboard so people can play against each other and share scores. It's also the same game per day, allowing people to improve their scores and try to get a spot on the daily leaderboard.

Click "Help" then "Walk me through my first trade" for a quick start.

I'd love to get some players on there and get some feedback. I hope whoever plays it enjoys it.

title.value: Show HN: Trade Lord, inspired by Drug Lord 2, quick daily leaderboard game

story_text.value:
Hi all,

I've been working on this app for a few months now, and I think it's at a stage where I can share it with everyone.

I built this app because AI-assisted coding is here to stay. With the right harness, AI can handle many things that were previously difficult. It can even perform PR reviews, in many ways better than humans. However:

> Code is only the visible part of a program. The real program is the understanding behind it: why it's built this way, how it maps to the business, and what breaks when you change it. That understanding lives in people, not in files.

Every day I slog through reviewing quite a few PRs containing dozens of file changes, and the only thing I had were file diffs. I struggled to build a complete picture of how all those different pieces connected. I'd jump between files and functions in my IDE, trying to piece together how they all fit.

So I built this tool to avoid hopping between different files and functions. You give it a PR, and it calculates the blast radius in the form of impacted or new user journeys. In those user journeys, you can see what was changed. You don't need to hop between different files, and for each step in the journey, you can go directly to the code. It provides full context in one single view.

A lot of the time I thought, "Okay, why do I need to build this thing? Claude can do it." Still, I was never happy with Claude's output, and I always found myself reaching for this tool. At some point I thought, "Why not just build it properly and share it with everyone?" This tool has helped me immensely with my understanding of the codebase.

Visualising code as a city is not the main goal of this tool, but I wanted to try it anyway. I think it's pretty cool. Sometimes, looking at the size, height, and width of a building gives me a feeling that maybe that class needs some refactoring.

I put a lot of effort into this. I do intend to sell it commercially, but before that, I wanted to see if people find it useful. Would love your feedback.

title.value: Show HN: LogPhase – See a PR's blast radius as impacted user journeys

story_text.value:
I built NIBIA Fabric, an open-source distributed LLM inference system that pools CPU and RAM across macOS, Linux, and Windows machines.

It builds on llama.cpp, with capacity-aware scheduling, adaptive memory reservation, persistent tensor caching, and an OpenAI-compatible API.

I’ve validated the current alpha on three physical machines across several models, including a 30B-class Qwen model, as well as GPT-OSS 20B. Feedback on the architecture and use cases is very welcome.
